title: Vibecoded a futuristic racer demo like many, but I stuck with it for 6 months now
author: ActionLittle4176
selftext:
Steam page: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5310180/Formula\_Minus\_One/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5310180/Formula_Minus_One/)  
Open beta: [https://fm1.app](https://fm1.app/)

\----

Some of you might remember [my post about the 32/64bit-style racing prototype](https://www.reddit.com/r/vibecoding/comments/1vvhi7t/vibe_coded_this_game_in_four_months/?pid=t3_1vvhi7t) I had built in four months. Yes, it's a genre you see a lot around here, because it's easy to get started with (until the next dopamine-driven prototype).

But I stuck with it.

And the improvement over the past two months has been tremendous, and you'll see that if you compare the two videos. Since the last post, I listened to your feedback and:

\* Threw every level in the bin and rebuilt them from scratch, then added new ones that are far bigger and more detailed. It felt like jumping a console generation, and it still runs on mobile.

\* Wrote a design and style guide for the game (semi-low poly characters and duotone as design signature), and redesigned the characters and menus to match it.

\* Kept pushing to make it my own thing rather than yet another clone-slop: adventure vibes, interaction with the environments, kinetic combat with combos…

\* Improved the handling and the readability.

And above all, and I think it shows in the trailer: I had a blast making it. If it had just been work, I wouldn't have gotten this far.

It's called Formula Minus One, and it launches on Steam first, in February. I'll keep improving it and adding content after that.

Half a year ago this was a prototype to experiment with, like so many others. Then I committed to making the best game I possibly could. Now I can finally see light at the end of the tunnel: yes, you can start a prototype, and yes, you can finish it.

There's still a lot of work ahead, so any feedback you can give me is very welcome.

 Here’s how I made it:

\* Code and tooling: frontier LLMs from OpenAI and Anthropic, with open-source models filling in the gaps and limiting the budget.

\* Characters, ships and environments: pencil sketch > GPT Gen 2 > Tripo to turn it into a 3D model > Blender to clean up the imperfections.

\* Sound: stock sound effects from Magnific. Music sketched out on a MIDI keyboard, final music generated with Suno.

\* Stack: Three.js, WebGPU, TypeScript, Rapier for physics. Nothing else, no Godot, no Unity…

I'm having a great time, but it's also hard work if you want to pay attention to every detail, and it's a very lonely experience. If the game sells well enough, I'd love to start paying artists and composers to replace the current assets and create new ones, and free up more time for what I really enjoy: directing and overall design.

\----

Steam page: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5310180/Formula\_Minus\_One/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5310180/Formula_Minus_One/)

Looking good. I wonder if 3js is a more common backend for Steam games than I realized. I've seen it said a lot that one needs Godot/Unity for "serious" dev work but this looks plenty serious.

I paid particular attention to your city + night scenes as I'm building something in that space (taxi stuff, not racing). I have at least some experience to compare it too in other words, and for those scenes/shots it looks very good indeed. Lots of detail already to things and lighting looks spot on.

https://preview.redd.it/5m6kfzqf54vh1.png?width=740&format=png&auto=webp&s=f573cdfccb5f8d500670b4bfd1937619bbdcc403

The apt (left) looks like it has some depth, near and distant buildings alike aren't single light blobs but varied greatly, the neon of signs and track edges blooms just right. What looks like a distant train and some billboards popping out slightly. This is all good stuff. Similar to things I've been trying to tackle so I can appreciate the work here even though we only see it for 0.05 seconds at a time :P

This looks great, OP. Fantastic work. It really shows you've put a lot of effort into it.

I'm super interested in how your terrain system works, anything special there?

replies.author: ActionLittle4176
replies.body:
Thanks! It’s a custom terrain system built with Three.js. I mix procedural noise with things like dunes, ridges and craters, then tweak the setup for each circuit.

The fun bit is that the terrain adapts around the track, carving out space for it while keeping valleys under bridges. A lot of the work is just making the textures feel less repetitive and keeping it all light enough to run on mobile 😅

comments.author: ZAPcon_64
comments.body:
The game looks pretty decent overall and the one track I played was pretty fun! the only big critique I really have other than some UI stuff is that the characters all feel super bland.   
  
Some of the racers look almost identical to each other but with slightly altered facial expressions (looking at Aditya and Dario for instance). Not sure how married you are to the designs, as you said that was your favorite part of the process, but I would suggest taking a step back and thinking about creating some more unique characters, whether that means adding new elements to the existing ones, or completely redesigning them from scratch to give them more personality.

I can see that you were definitely trying to make them all distinguishable from each other by adding people with different ethnic backgrounds, but they all just look so generic that they kind of blend together.   
  
I think even just adding some minor details (a headband here, a helmet there, you get a rebreather device, you get a metal cranium implant, etc) would go a LONG way in punching them up. For instance, you could take the Maori guy and take his traditional mouth tattoo to the cyberpunk extreme and give him a metal jaw/lower mouth that has an ivory look to it and is heavily engraved with the traditional inked Maori designs, maybe with a race car design hidden in it. That's just a suggestion of course lol Maybe stuff like that is too extreme for what you're going for. 

Otherwise, I say this is a pretty good job! Good luck on the rest of the journey!

replies.author: ActionLittle4176
replies.body:
Right! The character uniqueness is still work in progress (I really want the game be character driven more than ship driven), and I'm yet testing characters, backgrounds and the custom cockpits for every one (I'm planning a story mode).

Thanks for the good feedback!

comments.author: Opening_Wafer_6584
comments.body:
Hey! Alex here from the Tripo Studio US team. The jump from “prototype I’m experimenting with” to an actual February Steam launch is probably the most impressive part of this.

Also really interesting seeing the pencil sketch → image generation → Tripo → Blender pipeline applied consistently across characters, ships, and environments rather than just for one-off assets.

How much Blender cleanup are you typically doing now compared with when you started the project? Has that part of the workflow gotten faster as you’ve dialed in the art direction?

replies.author: ActionLittle4176
replies.body:
Hi! Thank you so much for your kind words. Without Tripo, I wouldn't have been able to make the game look the way it does.

For me, the real game-changer these past few weeks was using Tripo via the API, because it fit seamlessly into my workflow with the LLM. This way, I was able to give the LLM a detailed plan and level designs, and the LLM created half the level on its own, using GPT Gen, Tripo, and Blender autonomously. After that, it was just a matter of iterating.

Tripo’s P2 model is currently the best for geometry with fewer than 25,000 triangles, and this is a game where I’m very disciplined about geometry so it can run on mobile devices. It produces fewer imperfections than the P1 model, and the LLM is able to detect and correct them using Blender. P2 it's also great for creating lower-poly versions of large models for when they're viewed from a distance (LOD).
